Neonatal Bluespotted stingrays emerge from their egg cases at a disc width of approximately 11 cm [Lb = approximately 11 cm], a size that reflects the considerable yolk reserves allocated during internal gestation. This birth dimension is modest relative to the ultimate disc width attained by adults, which can reach 40.2 cm [Li = 40.2 cm] in females, a value estimated from extensive field measurements of mature individuals across their Indo-Pacific range. Males, however, are sexually dimorphic in their maximum size, achieving a somewhat smaller ultimate disc width of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm]. This difference in asymptotic dimensions likely relates to the energetic demands of reproduction; females must accommodate developing embryos within their body cavity, placing a premium on larger body size. Growth trajectories in Neotrygon kuhlii are characterized by relatively rapid expansion during the first few years of life, followed by a gradual plateau as individuals approach their asymptotic dimensions, a pattern common among batoids of similar ecological guild.

The onset of reproductive capability in Bluespotted stingrays is signaled by specific size thresholds rather than by age alone. Puberty in the population as a whole has been estimated at a disc width of 28 cm [Lp = 28 cm], a size at which gonadal maturation typically commences. Males appear to reach sexual maturity at a slightly smaller disc width of 26.5 cm [Lp = 26.5 cm], reflecting the reduced somatic investment required for male reproductive function compared to the demands of gestation in females. These values were derived from macroscopic and histological examination of gonadal tissue from a large sample of specimens collected throughout the year in Australian waters. Attainment of these disc widths generally occurs between two and three years of age under favorable conditions, though local variation in prey availability can shift this timing considerably. The size-based nature of maturation in this species, like many elasmobranchs, underscores the importance of reaching a critical body dimension before allocating resources to reproduction.

Under stable thermal conditions typical of tropical reef habitats, specifically at a water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C], the gestation period of Neotrygon kuhlii lasts approximately 305 days [ab = approximately 305 days]. This extended developmental interval, nearly ten months in duration, is characteristic of many small-to-medium dasyatid rays and reflects the production of relatively well-developed pups. The 305 day gestation is followed by parturition of one to two pups per litter [N_R_i = one to two pups per litter], with females typically giving birth only once each year [F_R_i = birth only once each year]. This low annual fecundity, combined with the protracted gestation, contributes to the species' relatively slow population growth rate and makes it particularly susceptible to overexploitation. The combination of small litter size and long gestation places Neotrygon kuhlii among the less productive elasmobranchs, with a maximum annual reproductive output of one or two offspring per female [Ri = annual reproductive output of one or two offspring per female].

Adult body mass in Bluespotted stingrays shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, mirroring the pattern observed in disc width. The ultimate wet weight recorded for females reaches approximately 2024.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 2024.7 grams], a mass that represents the upper range of body sizes observed in mature individuals from the Coral Sea and Great Barrier Reef populations. Males are considerably lighter, with an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1229 grams [Wwi = approximately 1229 grams]. This nearly 40% reduction in maximum mass relative to females is consistent with the female-larger size dimorphism common in dasyatid rays, where abdominal cavity volume directly constrains fecundity. The mass data were collected during routine tagging and release programs conducted by fisheries researchers, with individuals weighed using spring scales to the nearest gram. These values likely represent near-asymptotic masses, as both sexes were captured within the size range where growth in disc width has largely ceased.

Longevity in Neotrygon kuhlii has been estimated at approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under natural conditions, a lifespan that aligns well with those reported for other small dasyatid rays inhabiting warm, stable environments at a temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. This estimate, derived from vertebral growth-band analysis and tag-recapture studies, was obtained from populations experiencing a mean annual water temperature of 27.8 °C [T = 27.8 °C]. The relatively extended lifespan, when paired with the species' low fecundity and delayed maturation, positions it as a classic K-selected strategist among elasmobranchs. Such life-history traits render Neotrygon kuhlii particularly vulnerable to even modest increases in adult mortality from fishing pressure or habitat degradation. The combination of a long generation time, small litter size, and late age at maturity means that population recovery from overexploitation can take several decades, emphasizing the need for careful, precautionary management of this attractive and ecologically important benthic predator.
